body_markdown:
Unfortunately, car-based pickups—or “utes” as our more enlightened Australian brethren call them—didn’t quite catch on in America. Australians had a whole host of Ford, Valiant, and Holden utilities to choose from, including muscular variants and flatbed work horses. There are also a few compact models currently available in the markets south of our border. As for America, Ford pioneered the category with the[Ranchero](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=1957+ford+ranchero) in 1957 and Chevrolet followed in 1959 with the[El Camino](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=1959+chevrolet+el+camino) .


There were also compacts like the Subaru Brat and Dodge Rampage for a while, but Ford and Chevy dominated what little market there was to be had here. Ranchero was based on the full-size lineup for 1957–59, the compact Falcon from 1960–65, and finally the mid-size Fairlane/Torino platform until its final model year in 1979. GM followed a similar pattern, moving to the compact Nova in the early ‘60s before using the mid-size Chevelle and then introducing a rebadged GMC version, called[Sprint](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=gmc+sprint) and then[Caballero](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=gmc+caballero) .


And then there’s this Pontiac Star Chief. It didn’t leave the factory as a pickup in 1958, and indeed Pontiac never built production car-based pickups, but it has us thinking about all of the fantastic coupe utilities that could have been.


Hagerty Marketplace


Hagerty Marketplace


The “Pontimino” was a part of Greg Rusk’s “[Generous Collection](https://www.hagerty.com/marketplace/collections/the-generous-collection) ” that has been selling on Hagerty Marketplace. It recently changed hands for $48,418, falling within the[#2 (excellent) range for a 370-powered Star Chief Safari wagon](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/pontiac/star_chief/1958/1958-pontiac-star_chief-safari?id=aCn1I000000CuYSSA0&condition=excellent) , on which this custom is based.


It’s the product of Myles Miller, who cut up the wagon and melded its sheet metal into a very convincing rendition of what GM could have done in 1958. Of course, Miller went above and beyond. The car is not just customized into a utility; he shaved the handles, grafted in 1959 Cadillac bullet taillights, Frenched the rear bumper, inserted 1957 Corvette grille teeth, and laid down a custom paint job with scallops and plenty of pinstriping. What strikes us is just how well the factory lines of the Pontiac’s quarter panels lend themselves to bedsides. It’s really not that far off the jet-inspired 1958 Chevrolet and GMC[Fleetside](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=1958+fleetside) pickup beds.


A 370-cubic-inch Pontiac V-8 lives under the hood, just as you’d expect in a 1958 Star Chief Safari. This one is topped by an Edelbrock four-barrel carb and a bat wing-style air cleaner painted and pinstriped to match the exterior.


Hagerty Marketplace


Looking at a ‘50s Pontiac coupe utility, we can’t help but imagine such a thing actually going into series production. GM had several brands to work with, each with different design language, some of them better suited to a utility than others. Still, the only factory versions GM ever offered that weren’t El Caminos came with the same sheet metal styling. There have been several attempts made by various customizers, and even GM tempted us with several versions of a Pontiac with a bed, most recently with an imported version of the Australian-built GT. It never came to fruition.


Hagerty Marketplace


Hagerty Marketplace


Inspired by a B-17 bomber, the steering wheel was cut down into a yoke. Silver and purple upholstery match the dash, which also features blue highlights like the exterior.


Imagine if Pontiac had run with the utility body style and given the El Camino some internal competition. It’s easy to picture various GTO body styles with a pickup bed. We have a feeling a 1969 GTO Judge utility in Carousel Red with hidden headlights would be every bit as collectible as its coupe counterpart. AMC was scrappy and adapted a lot of body styles from the same underpinnings, yet never built a Rambler ute. Mopar had the guts to do wild things in the ’60s and ’70s, yet we never got a Road Runner with a bed, either. That’s a shame. How about Buick? A 455-powered GS with a bed seems viable. Then there’s the G-body era. Enthusiasts have swapped[Grand National](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/buick/regal/1987/1987-buick-regal-grand_national?id=aCn1I000000Ct4lSAC) front ends and powerplants into ‘80s El Caminos. Even when bench-racing the possibilities, we have to admit that a Grand National utility would have been a tiny market, but we appreciate that it has been done.

Back to the Pontimino, we’re glad that it found someone who appreciates the big swings it took to see this project to completion. It can be difficult to sell a car as highly customized as this, as the more extreme the modification, the smaller the potential buyer pool tends to be. The audacious concept of this car had loads of potential, but also plenty of off-ramps that could have led to disaster. Our hats are off to Myles Miller for pulling off such a huge undertaking and hopefully inspiring others to take on similarly lofty projects. If you’re a ute fan, let us know which never-built utility you’d like to see.
